items.title: Mindweave 3.2.8: MCP servers that stay connected, Ctrl+X to background a command, and selecting while you scroll
items.summary: An agent that added an MCP server could be told it was not connected while it was running fine. That is fixed, and MCP calls now fold into one row with the commands and reads. Ctrl+X moves a running command to the background, a text selection keeps growing while you scroll, and a few frames that flashed the wrong picture are gone. The mwcode app gets this with its next release.
points: A tool call finds its MCP server when it runs, so restarting a server no longer breaks the calls after it.
The agent can check a server and restart it without asking, and a slow tool is allowed ten minutes.
MCP calls fold into the work row, one line each, with the server's own reason when one fails.
Ctrl+X moves the command the agent is waiting on to the background.
Drag to select and keep scrolling: the selection keeps growing and copies all of it.

sections.text: The tools a turn offered were tied to the connection that existed when the turn began. Enabling, disabling or adding a server replaces that connection, so every call after it failed with not connected for the rest of the turn, and the agent's own attempts to restart the server made it certain. A call now looks up the live connection, brings a server that died back up, and a server added during the turn can be called in that turn.

sections.h: The agent can look, and restart
list: Two new actions, status and reconnect, need no question. Enabling a server that is already running changes nothing, and enable says whether it connected and why not.
A tool call has ten minutes instead of the thirty seconds meant for the protocol's own bookkeeping, so a tool doing real work can finish.
Esc stops a tool call that is waiting on a server, and the server is told to cancel it.
The repeated failure stop notices an agent alternating between restarting a server and calling it.
They fold into the work row with commands and reads, such as Called 3 MCP tools, managed 1 MCP server, with a mark for each.
Every line has the same shape: a mark, the name, and what happened. A call that worked shows how long it took. One that failed shows the server's own reason.
Click a call to see what it asked and what came back. A change you declined shows as declined.
A server's prompts no longer fill the command menu. Type after the slash to find them.

sections.h: Ctrl+X: a command to the background, yourself
sections.text: After a couple of seconds the command's own line offers Ctrl+X. Press it and the command keeps running as a background shell and the agent carries on. It is told you moved it, and told when the command ends. It works on a command that would not be moved on its own, and every command running at that moment moves.

list: A selection that starts in the conversation keeps growing while you turn the wheel, or while you hold the pointer past the top or bottom edge.
Letting go copies everything it covered, including what scrolled out of sight, and Ctrl+C copies it again.
If a flick scrolls so fast that a row was never drawn, it tells you that part was not copied.
Opening the newest row moves the view just far enough to show what opened, and folding it puts the view back.
Opening a row, or typing a slash for the menu, used to flash the wrong picture for a frame. With the view at the bottom the conversation is now lined up with the bottom by the layout itself.
The model picker still draws an empty box for about one frame before its items appear.
The selection only follows the conversation in the fullscreen shell. The inline shell leaves selecting to the terminal.

sections.text: The terminal inside the app gets all of this when the app itself is next updated.

items.title: Mindweave 3.2.7: edits show only what changed, and macOS and Linux are supported
items.summary: An edit used to fill a screen with the old text in red and the new text in green. Now only the lines that changed are marked, with line numbers and the changed words highlighted. The test suite, the typecheck and the build now run on macOS and Linux on every change, and several things that quietly did not work on a Mac are fixed. The mwcode app gets this with its next release.
points: An edit shows only the lines that changed, with line numbers and two lines of context.
Changed words inside a rewritten line are marked, each change on its own.
The test suite runs on macOS (Apple silicon) and Linux on every change, next to Windows.
Running processes read as stopped on a Mac, copying on Linux, and the Option and Alt word keys are fixed.

sections.text: An edit used to be drawn as the old text in red and then the new text in green, so a paragraph that only gained two lines was shown twice and took a screen. Now the file before and after is compared. Only the lines that changed are marked, the lines around them are dim context, and each line has its number. A gap between two groups of changes is one dim row. The words that differ between a removed line and the line that replaced it are marked a step brighter, each change on its own.

list: The preview shows up to thirty rows, and a click shows the rest.
An opened block wraps a long line under itself with the number column kept.
The header now counts what really changed. It said minus 26 plus 58 for a two-line addition, because it counted the text of each replacement.
Replacing a symbol and rewriting a file show the same comparison. A new file shows numbered additions.
A terminal with 256 colours, such as Apple's Terminal.app, gets tints chosen for it, and a 16-colour terminal relies on the sign and the text colour.
A row of one command folds when you click the opened box. Only its header was clickable.
A command ended from outside, such as the agent restarting the app it is testing, no longer prints a red exit minus 1 line as if it had crashed.
An edit that failed quietly no longer splits the reads around it into two rows.

The suite, the typecheck and the build run on macOS (Apple silicon) and Linux on every change, and a failure on either fails the build. The packed package is also installed into a clean folder and its commands are run.
On a Mac every running process was read as stopped, so a running language server looked shut down. That is fixed.
Pages in the browser the ui tool drives now open on a slow machine, and deleting a system folder is refused on a Mac and on more Linux folders.
Copying works on Linux desktops (X11 as well as Wayland) and in tmux, and leaves the clipboard of an SSH machine alone.
Option and Alt with the arrows move by a word, and Alt and D delete the word ahead. Only the Windows keys were bound before.
Driving another program's window by its title, and window screenshots, are still Windows only. Driving a web page or a dev server works everywhere.
How it looks in Terminal.app, iTerm2, GNOME Terminal and Konsole has not been checked by eye, and it has not been run on an Intel Mac.
A change too large to compare cheaply still shows the old text and the new text, and a session saved by an older version draws its diffs the way they were saved.

sections.text: The terminal inside the app gets all of this when the app itself is next updated.

items.title: Mindweave 3.2.6: long sessions stay fast, and a very long one reopens quickly
items.summary: A session of a few hundred messages could make scrolling drop frames and typing lag, and reopening it did not help. That is fixed: scrolling costs the same from a short session to a 25,000-message one, and a session that took 28 seconds to reopen now takes about 2. The mwcode app gets this with its next release.
points: Scrolling no longer slows down once a session passes 600 blocks.
A 25,000-message session reopens in about 2 seconds instead of 28.
A 10,000-message session reopens in 1.6 seconds instead of 7.5.
Memory stays flat however long you scroll.

sections.text: The screen draws only the blocks in view and stands in a spacer of the right height for the rest, which needs the height of every block. The table of heights was capped at 600, a number from when the scrollback held 150 blocks, while the scrollback holds 10,000. Past 600 the oldest height was dropped, and the screen then laid out every block on every frame, measuring and redrawing without ever settling. That is why a long session stayed slow even after it was closed and reopened.

list: On the real app, a wheel notch costs about the same from a 100-message session to a 25,000-message one.
Memory stays flat across thousands of notches.
Scrolling all the way up through very old history reaches your first message and shows no blank gaps.
Each tool call copied the record of every call the session had ever made. It now keeps only the calls whose rows are still open, which also makes each call in a long live session cheaper.
Each message you sent copied the whole history to stamp a few wait times. It now copies only when a row needs one.

Every old message was laid out in full on the first frame, only to learn its height. Now only the newest 300 are, and older ones take an estimated height that is replaced by the real one when they come near the window.
The scrollable length can shift slightly the first time you scroll through very old history, until those messages have been measured. What is drawn is never affected.
This was tested on Windows and has not been run on a real Mac yet.

sections.text: The terminal inside the app gets all of this when the app itself is next updated.

items.title: Mindweave 3.2.4 and 3.2.5: Lightning stops asking, and sub-agents become a rare tool
items.summary: Lightning now runs commands without asking, and a sub-agent that runs out of steps still reports what it found. The agent does ordinary work and its own checks itself instead of starting sub-agents, and a verifier that answers in prose shows how many commands it ran. The mwcode app gets this with its next release.
points: Lightning runs commands without asking. Sentinel is the mode that asks.
A sub-agent that runs out of steps is given one last turn to say what it found.
The agent runs its own tests and checks. A sub-agent is for a genuinely large job, or when you ask.
A verifier that answers in prose shows `ran 5 commands`, not `0 checks`.

sections.h: Lightning does not ask about commands (3.2.4)
list: Force-pushing, a hard reset, git clean, deleting a branch, publishing a package and running code downloaded from the internet used to ask in every mode. Now they only ask in Sentinel, even after allow all commands.
Stopping a program by name asks in no mode. 3.2.3 said it asked first, and that was a mistake: the agent restarts the app it is testing after almost every build.
A rule you wrote yourself to ask about a command is still asked. That is your own word.
A few questions that are not about the work stay in every mode: a file that runs code later, a project's own tool servers, and writing outside the folders you opened.
A command that is refused whatever you answer, such as one already running in the background or one with a guaranteed parse error, is refused before any question.

sections.h: A sub-agent that runs out of steps still reports (3.2.4)
sections.text: Before, a sub-agent that reached its step limit returned only a pause note written for a person, and everything it had read and run was thrown away. In one session a verifier spent thirty steps on eight checks and returned nothing. Now it is given one last turn, with no tools, to say what it checked and what it did not get to. A verifier also gets 40 steps by default instead of 20, and the line on screen says Stopped at its step limit.

list: The block in the conversation holds the question and what it is about, and a dim allowed or declined line follows once you answer.
The working line stops counting while a question waits for you, and says Waiting for your answer.

sections.text: In one session the agent started four verifier sub-agents for ordinary work, one only to re-check its own fixes. The cause was the built-in instructions, which told it to check any non-trivial work with a separate verifier and to run it again after fixing what it found. Now the agent does ordinary work itself: reading, searching, editing, running the tests and the build, and checking its own result. A sub-agent is for a job that is genuinely large, such as a sweep over a big codebase, or for when you ask. A verifier is for high-risk work, such as something about to be published, and it is used once. The tool's own description now lists what not to hand it.

A verifier that answered in plain prose showed Failed verification, 0 checks, even when it had run the project's checks and several probes, because only lines written in the dollar-command form were counted. It now says how many commands it ran. The verdict itself is unchanged.

list: Lightning runs what the agent decides to run. What goes wrong is yours to answer for, so use Sentinel when you want to be asked.
Fewer sub-agents means fewer tokens spent, and the agent's own checks show up in the conversation as ordinary commands.
This was tested on Windows and has not been run on a real Mac yet.

sections.text: The terminal inside the app gets all of this when the app itself is next updated.

items.title: Mindweave 3.2.3: sub-agents read at a glance, and a check has to be a real check
items.summary: A sub-agent is now a short title and how it ended, with its calls a click away. A verifier can run the tests it is asked to run, and its verdict is checked against what it really did. The model keeps the edits it just wrote, a screenshot no longer photographs the terminal, and the app driver says when a port is not yours. The mwcode app gets this with its next release.
points: A sub-agent is a title and an answer: a tick when it worked, a cross when it failed, a bang when it only half worked.
A verifier can run builds, tests and the app, and a check only counts if its command really ran.
The model keeps its own recent edits instead of having them cleared from its memory.
A screenshot with no window named never takes a picture of the terminal.

sections.text: A sub-agent used to show as its whole task pasted onto one line, cut off in the middle of a word, then every call it made, then a summary written for the agent and not for you. Now it is a short title taken from the task, and how it ended: a tick, a cross, or a bang when it could only do part of it, with the number of steps and how long it took. While it works the dot pulses and the line says what it is doing.

list: Click it to see a shaded band with the task, the result, a count of what it did, and each call.
A call that came back again and again, such as checking on a background program, is one line with a count.
A call it was refused is red.
Several at once are one group, each with its own two lines, so you can see who is doing what and how far along.

sections.h: Why a verifier was not worth much before
sections.text: A verifier is a second agent that checks work the first one did. It was told to run the tests, but it was made read-only like any research worker, which took away the ability to run anything. So it read the code, wrote down what it would have tested, and put PASS next to it. In one real session its report said it had made eight checks, and one of its PASS lines was wrong. Nothing in Mindweave could tell the difference between a check it ran and one it only described.

list: A verifier can now run builds, tests, the typechecker, scripts that call the code, and the app. It still cannot edit or write files.
It is refused, with the reason, anything that deletes, moves or copies files, changes a git repository, installs or publishes packages, stops processes, or writes anywhere but the temporary folder.
Each check in its report is compared with the commands it really ran. A check whose command never ran does not count, and the PASS under it says so.
If a project file changed while it ran, a pass becomes a partial, the file is named, and undo can put it back.
Whatever it started in the background is stopped when it finishes.

The model keeps what it wrote. When an old tool result was cleared to save space, the edit that produced it was cleared too, and the model was left remembering only its last two or three edits. It now keeps up to forty of its recent edits, or about 24,000 tokens of them, newest first.
The app driver tells the model when a debugging port belongs to a program it did not start, with the page title, so it does not mistake another application for the one it is testing.
A screenshot taken without naming a window used to photograph whichever window had focus, which was almost always the terminal Mindweave runs in. It now says so and lists the other windows.
Stopping every program with a given name, such as every Electron app, now asks first.

sections.h: How this makes it better, and what to know
list: Fewer false "verified" results, because a check has to be a command that ran.
Fewer mistakes from the model contradicting code it wrote a few minutes earlier.
Fewer wrong-app and wrong-window mistakes when testing an app.
It costs something: a verifier takes longer and uses more, and keeping edits adds up to about 24,000 tokens to a request, most of it cheap cached input.

A script that deletes a file by itself cannot be seen from the command line. It is caught afterwards by looking at the project files, which cannot put back a file over 256 KB or one outside the project.
This was tested on Windows and has not been run on a real Mac yet. The checks are proven in tests; how much a real model improves over a long session has not been measured yet.

sections.text: The terminal inside the app gets all of this when the app itself is next updated.

items.title: Mindweave 3.2.2: a UI test is one line, and what you open sits on a band
items.summary: When the agent tests an app, every look, click and typed word used to be a row of its own, each with a long list of the page. They now fold into one line like Tested 5 steps, with a mark for each step, and the dot pulses while it works. What you open sits on a shaded band, and a line that holds a single call opens in one click. The mwcode app gets this with its next release.
points: The steps of a UI test fold into one line, with a mark for each step.
A step that failed says why on its own line, in red, without opening anything.
What you open sits on a shaded band, like a message you wrote.
A line holding only one command or one step opens in one click, not two.

sections.text: Testing an app used to leave a row for every look, click and typed word, and each row carried its own list of every control on the page. A test of seven steps was a hundred lines. Now the steps fold into the same line as the commands and reads, like Tested 5 steps, with one mark per step. The dot pulses while the test runs, and the line says which step it is on, so a long test does not look stuck.

list: Click the line to list the steps, one line each. Click a step to see what it did and what the page looked like.
The page is shown by kind, such as button with the names beside it, instead of sixteen numbered lines. The numbers were for the agent, not for you.
A step that failed keeps its reason on the line, in red. Before, a failure printed the whole page every time.
If the line holds a single command or a single step, it opens straight onto it. With two or more, each opens on its own click.

sections.h: A clearer look when something is open
list: The text you open sits on a shaded band, the same shade as a message you wrote, with no vertical line. The line you opened is bright and the others stay dim, so you can tell which one is open.
Long lines wrap inside the band, and every row of it is the full width.

sections.text: A command that printed a carriage return, which PowerShell does, could break the band, because a terminal sends the cursor back to the left edge. Output is now cleaned before it is drawn.

list: /help now says that tests fold too.
Older chats open the same way, and a write or edit saved without its full text is put back together from the file when you reopen the chat.

sections.text: The terminal inside the app gets all of this when the app itself is next updated. This was tested on Windows. It has not been run on a real Mac yet.

items.title: Mindweave 3.2.1: quick fixes, more help, and Claude Haiku 5.5
items.summary: A round of quick fixes for the terminal, more help built in, and Claude Haiku 5.5 added to the model list. The agent's session notes are now used only when a conversation is cut down, so they can no longer disagree with the conversation it is in. The mwcode app gets this with its next release.
points: Claude Haiku 5.5 is in /model: the fastest and cheapest, for quick, simple work.
/help now explains the folded lines like Ran 3 commands, and how to open them.
The agent's session notes can no longer contradict what it just did.
A long command and its note no longer run into each other.

list: The agent's notes about a session used to be shown to it on every turn. If they fell behind, a small model could end up arguing with its own memory. They are now used only when a conversation is cut down, and they are kept up to date while the work is going on.
A long command no longer runs into the note beside it. The note goes on its own line when it does not fit.
Lines that repeated what a row already showed, such as a note that a command was killed, are gone. A command that died on its own with an error, or went quiet, is still reported.
Pointing at a long output now changes only its click to show line. The rest stays still.
/help explains what a line like Ran 3 commands, read 2 files means, and how to open it with a click or Ctrl+O.
It also says how to scroll back and how to get back to the end.
The tip line mentions that a line ending in an arrow opens when you click it.
Pick it in /model. Haiku 4.5 is still there.
Thinking can be turned off on it, but only at effort high or below.
A prompt over 100,000 tokens costs five times the rate on this model, so Mindweave compacts the conversation at 100,000 tokens on it instead of letting a long session cross that line.

sections.text: The terminal inside the app gets all of this when the app itself is next updated.

items.title: Mindweave 3.2.0: what the agent runs and reads folds into one line
items.summary: Everything the agent runs or reads between two things you can see now takes one line, like Ran 3 commands, read 3 files. Click it to see each command and which lines of each file were read. Long output, writes and edits open in place with a click, and scrolling is steadier.
points: Commands and reads share one folded line, with a mark for how each command ended.
Click to open the list, click a command to see what it printed.
Reads say which part of the file they took, such as lines 410 to 551.
Long output, whole-file writes and edits open on a click and fold on the next.

sections.h: One line for the agent's working
sections.text: Commands and file reads used to stack up as a row each. Now they fold into one line that says how many commands ran and how many files were read. A red mark shows a failed command without opening anything, and the dot pulses while something is still working.

list: Click the line to list every command and every file read.
Click a command to see what it printed. Click again to fold it.
A read shows the file and the part it took: the lines, the whole file, or that it was read before.
Hovering lights up what you are over. Nothing is underlined.
A long command output, a whole-file write or an edit shows the start and a line to open the rest.
Your chats keep the full text of writes and edits, even after old context is cleared, and old chats open the same way.
A long line wraps instead of being cut when a row is open.
Each wheel step moves the same few lines, with no animation, so you keep your place.
The scrolled-back chip shows how far through the chat you are.

items.title: Mindweave 3.1.0 and mwcode 1.0.5: safer by default, fewer questions, your own hooks
items.summary: Opening a project can no longer start programs or reach your secrets, harmless commands stop asking for permission, and you can set your own rules and hooks. The app adds screens for them, smoother scrolling and Ollama as a normal provider.
points: Opening a project no longer starts the servers it names. You are shown the command and asked.
Sentinel stops asking about commands that only read, and you can answer never ask again for one like npm test.
Your own command rules and hooks, kept where a cloned project cannot reach them.
Smoother scrolling, Ollama as a normal provider, and long sessions cost less.

list: Servers named in a project's own config wait for your answer before they start, and a project cannot swap one of yours.
Helpers such as language servers say where they come from and ask before they are installed.
Files that run code later, such as a commit hook or a CI workflow, ask before the agent writes them.
Protected files are judged by the file itself, so a link or a different spelling of the path does not get around them. Copying or sending one with a shell command is refused.
The agent cannot save its own rules or lift a protection without showing you the text and asking.
Text you cannot see, hidden in a note, a file or a web page, is removed before the model reads it.

sections.h: Fewer questions that do not matter
list: Commands that only read, such as ls, cat and git status, no longer ask in Sentinel.
Answer never ask again for a command like npm test and it is remembered for the project. You can take it back in Settings, Permissions.
Write your own rules: allow, always ask, or forbid a command, with a reason the agent is told.

sections.text: Run your own commands before or after a tool, when you send a message, when the agent finishes and when a chat starts. A hook can stop an action and tell the agent why. They live in your own settings folder, never in a project, so a cloned repository cannot add one.

list: Settings, Permissions now has Command rules and shows your hooks.
Settings, Tokens shows how much of your spend was background work you did not ask for, and what the current chat has done.
Marathon shows what a goal has cost against its ceiling.
Scrolling follows the system, and the app's own glides take the same time on every screen.
Ollama is a normal provider with its own page, and can run on another computer.
Session notes are no longer sent on every call when nothing has been cleared yet.
The task list survives a resume, a stalled stream is retried, and a reply cut off by the output limit carries on by itself.
A fast command could hang for two minutes on Linux. That is fixed.

sections.text: The app updates itself: press Update when it appears. For the terminal, run npm install -g mindweave@latest, or let the app do it from Settings, About. Both were tested on Windows and Linux. Neither has been run on a real Mac yet.

items.title: mwcode 1.0.2 is out
items.summary: Updates now install silently on Windows, the terminal version is judged by the copy you really run, and an npm install updates from inside the app.
points: Updating on Windows no longer shows the installer. If mwcode is installed for all users, Windows asks for permission once, then the update installs quietly and the app reopens.
The terminal version is judged by the copy you actually run, so you are not told about updates you already have. If you installed it with npm, press Update and mwcode runs npm for you.
The About page no longer shows a wrong command line version. Update from Settings, then About, or the Update available button at the top.

list: Updates on Windows install silently. One Windows permission prompt for an all-users install, then no setup window.
A terminal update notice only shows when the copy you run is out of date. The terminal that comes with the app moves with the app.
An npm install updates from inside the app. If npm cannot do it, the message says why in plain words.
On macOS the check waits for your real PATH, so Homebrew and nvm installs are found. On Linux the .deb command is recognised as the app’s own.
News from the same day appears in the order it was published, newest on top.

sections.text: Updating from 1.0.0 or 1.0.1 is carried out by the version you have now, so you may see the installer window once more. From 1.0.2 on, updates are silent.

items.title: mwcode 1.0.1 is out
items.summary: The app now knows which terminal version you really run, and an npm install can be updated without leaving the app.
points: The terminal version is judged by the copy you type in a terminal, not the one inside the app, so you are no longer told about updates you already have.
Installed it with npm? Press Update and mwcode runs npm for you. No browser, no copying a command.
Works on Windows, macOS and Linux. The app updates itself: Settings, then About, then Update, then restart.

list: A terminal update notice only shows when the copy you actually run is out of date.
The terminal that comes with the app moves with the app, so it never shows its own update notice.
An npm install updates from inside the app. If npm cannot do it, the message says why in plain words, and you can still copy the command.
On macOS the check waits for your real PATH, so Homebrew and nvm installs are found. On Linux the .deb command is recognised as the app’s own.
News from the same day now appears in the order it was published, newest on top.

items.title: Mindweave 3.0.1 is out
items.summary: A small update to 3.0: the terminal now shows its name as Mindweave 2, in the header, on the first-run screen and in --help. The version is still 3.0.
points: Nothing else changed. If 3.0.0 works for you, there is no hurry.
It matters only if you installed the terminal version with npm. The app has its own copy, which updates with the app.

sections.text: If you installed it with npm, run npm install -g mindweave@latest, or type /update inside Mindweave and it updates and reopens on the conversation you were in. Mindweave needs Node 24 or newer.

items.title: Mindweave 3.0.0 is out
items.summary: The biggest terminal release so far: a much faster screen, steps you can watch as they happen, goals that run on their own, usage limits, rewind, and local models through Ollama.
points: Scrolling and startup are much faster, and long conversations can be scrolled all the way back.
Each step shows up while it works: a running command pulses with its output underneath.
/marathon, /rewind, usage limits and Ollama are all new.
It needs Node 24 or newer. The app brings its own, so this only matters for npm installs.

list: Scrolling a long conversation takes about 70% less processor time, and it starts about 15% sooner than 2.5.1.
The mouse wheel speeds up the faster you turn it, and slow turns still move three lines.
The whole conversation can be scrolled now, not just the last part of it.
A row appears when a tool starts, with a pulsing dot, and settles when it finishes.
A command starts when its row appears, so you see it running with its output, not just the result.
Several reads fold into one row, and each step gets a moment on screen before the next one.
Starting an app or a server now reports how it went once, within a few seconds.
/marathon: hand over a goal and it keeps going until the goal is checked and done, it gets stuck, or it runs out of budget.
/rewind: go back to before one of your messages, files included, and edit it.
Usage limits per five hours, week or month, in tokens or money, and a view of what you have spent.
Testing an app by using it: it can open your app, click through it and read the screen.
Ollama: local models on your own machine, no key needed.
/app: get the desktop app, which shares sessions and settings with the terminal.
The colours now match the desktop app, and your own messages sit on a grey band.
Your message lines up with the agent's, and the gap under the header is gone.
New models, a check of the whole agent loop that fixed four faults, and better handling of long sessions.

sections.text: The terminal version inside mwcode is already up to date, so there is nothing to do there. If you also installed it with npm, run npm install -g mindweave@latest, or type /update inside Mindweave. It needs Node 24 or newer.

items.title: Getting started with mwcode
items.summary: A short guide to your first session, the three modes, the safety nets, and a few habits that make the agent a lot more useful.
points: Open a project folder, add a key or pick a local model, and ask for something small first.
Lightning just does it, Architect plans without touching anything, Sentinel asks before each change.
You can always go back: rewind to an earlier message, and keep your work in git.
Tell us what breaks with Send feedback in the sidebar. Every message is read.

list: Open a project folder. mwcode works inside it: it reads your files, edits them and runs commands there.
Add a key in Settings, then Providers. Keys stay on your computer and only go to the provider you picked.
No key? Install Ollama and pick one of its models. It runs on your own machine and costs nothing.
Start small. Ask it to explain the project, or to fix one thing you already know about. You will learn how it works faster than by reading about it.

sections.text: There is no single best one. Quick, cheap models are good for everyday edits and questions. Stronger models are worth it for hard bugs and bigger changes. Local models through Ollama keep everything on your machine, at the cost of speed and some quality. Switching is one click in the model menu under the message box, so try a few and keep what suits you.

list: Lightning: it goes ahead and does the work. Fastest, best when you trust the task.
Architect: it reads and plans but changes nothing. Good for understanding a codebase or agreeing on a plan first.
Sentinel: it asks before every change and every command. Good for unfamiliar projects or anything risky.

sections.text: Every step shows up in the chat as it happens: what it read, what it changed, and the commands it runs, with their output while they run. You can keep typing while it works. Your message waits its turn, and you can pull it back to edit it.

list: Rewind: take the conversation back to before one of your messages, files included, and go a different way.
Keep your project in git and commit before big changes. It is the simplest undo there is.
It makes mistakes, mostly depending on the model. Read what it changed before you rely on it.
Run starts your project's command and shows its output, so you and the agent can both see whether it works.
Marathon takes a goal and keeps going on its own until the goal is checked and done, it gets stuck, or it reaches its budget.
It can test an app by using it: opening it, clicking through and reading the screen, to tell an app that started from one that works.
Be specific. Name the file, the error, or what you expect to see.
Drop in a screenshot when something looks wrong. A picture explains a layout bug faster than words.
Keep notes about your project in MINDWEAVE.md. It is read at the start of every session.
Start a new session for a new task, so old context does not get in the way.

sections.text: Settings, then Tokens and usage limits, lets you cap what it uses per five hours, per week or per month, in tokens or in money. When a limit is reached it stops and tells you, instead of running on.

mwcode includes Mindweave, the terminal version of the same agent. Type mw in a terminal to use it. The Windows installer and the Linux .deb set that up for you, and on macOS you add it from Settings, then About. Both share the same sessions, keys and settings, so you can start in one and carry on in the other.

mwcode is young and gets better mostly through reports from people using it. Send feedback in the sidebar sends a message straight to the developer, no account needed. Bugs, ideas and things that felt confusing are all welcome.
